title: Opening principles
blurb: Three simple ideas get you through the first ten moves: fight for the centre, bring your pieces out, and castle.
deeperTitle: Why pick one opening; first ideas for White and Black

core.title: Three jobs for the first moves
body: Every game starts the same way. A good start follows three ideas:
**Centre.** Fight for the four middle squares.
**Develop.** Bring your knights and bishops out into the game.
**Castle.** Tuck your king away and wake up a rook.

core.prompt: Tap any one of the four centre squares.
core.explain: **d4, e4, d5 and e5.** Pieces standing here can see the most of the board.

core.title: Why the centre?
body: A piece in the middle sees more of the board. Look at this knight on e4: it attacks **eight** squares. Put the same knight on a1 and it reaches only **two**.
More squares means more options for you, and fewer for your opponent.

board.caption: The highlighted squares are the ones the knight attacks.

core.prompt: It is move one and you are White. Which move fights for the centre?
core.explain: A pawn on e4 claims the centre and opens lines for your bishop and queen. (A pawn to d4 is just as good.)

core.prompt: White played e4. Fight back for the centre.
core.hint: Which of your pawns or knights can challenge the middle?
core.explain: **e5** copies White and claims the middle. **d5**, **c5** and **Nf6** also challenge White's centre. Slow moves like a6 or h6 do not.

core.title: Develop your pieces
body: Your knights and bishops start behind the pawns, where they do nothing. **Developing** means moving them to squares where they see more.
Three habits: **knights before bishops**, **move each piece once**, and **keep the queen at home** for now.

core.prompt: White has played e4 and Nf3. Tap a White piece that still needs developing.
core.explain: The knight on b1 and both bishops are still asleep. Wake them up before you attack anything.

core.prompt: Develop a knight or a bishop. Leave the queen at home.
core.hint: Knights first is a good habit.
core.explain: **Nf3** is the classic: it develops a knight to a good square and attacks the e5 pawn. Any knight or bishop move follows the idea. Bringing the queen out does not.

core.prompt: White's knight attacks your e5 pawn. Defend it and develop in one move.
core.hint: A knight on the third rank guards e5.
core.explain: **Nc6** defends the pawn and develops a knight. That is two jobs in one move.

core.prompt: Why is it a mistake to bring your queen out early?
options: The queen is not allowed to move yet
Smaller pieces can attack her, and you lose time running away
core.explain: Every time a knight or bishop attacks your queen, she has to run, and your opponent gets a free developing move.

core.title: Castle early
body: Castling does two jobs at once: your king moves to safety and a rook joins the game.
You move the **king two squares** towards a rook, and the rook jumps over to the other side of him.
It is not allowed if the king or that rook has already moved, if pieces are in the way, or if the king is in check or would cross an attacked square.

board.caption: White is ready to castle kingside.

core.hint: Tap the king, then tap the square two steps to his right.
core.explain: **O-O** is how castling kingside is written. The rook hopped to f1 by itself.

core.prompt: Which opening start follows all three ideas?
core.explain: A centre pawn, then a knight, then a bishop. Next would come castling. The other two waste moves on the edge or bring the queen out too soon.

core.title: Punish an early queen
core.intro: Both players brought their queen out too soon. Take her.

puzzles.hint: A knight can attack a queen from far away.
puzzles.explain: Nothing protects the queen, so the knight wins her for free.
A knight is worth far less than a queen, so this trade is a gift.

deeper.title: Pick one opening and stick with it
body: An opening is just a well-tested way to follow the three ideas. You do not need a hundred of them.
Pick **one setup as White**, and **one reply to each first move as Black**. Play them again and again. You will learn the plans and the traps, and the first ten moves will start to feel easy.

deeper.title: A first idea for White: the Italian Game
body: Pawn to e4, knight to f3, bishop to c4. It claims the centre, develops two pieces, and points the bishop at f7. Castle next.

deeper.prompt: Play the first three White moves of the Italian Game: e4, Nf3, then Bc4. Black replies by itself.
deeper.hint: Pawn first, then the knight, then the bishop.
deeper.explain: That is the whole opening. The same three moves work against many replies.

deeper.prompt: Now find White's calm fourth move. Support the centre and free your bishop.
deeper.hint: A pawn move in front of the queen.
deeper.explain: **d3** props up the e4 pawn and opens the c1 bishop. **c3** is the other popular plan: it prepares d4.

deeper.title: A first idea for Black: copy the centre
body: When White plays **e4**, answer **e5**. When White plays **d4**, answer **d5**. Copying keeps the centre fair, and you can develop with the same ideas.

deeper.prompt: White opened with d4. Claim your share of the centre.
deeper.explain: **d5** copies White. **Nf6** is another good answer: it attacks the centre with a knight instead of a pawn.

deeper.prompt: You are Black in the Italian Game. Develop your bishop to the matching diagonal.
deeper.explain: **Bc5** mirrors White: a developed bishop, aiming at f2. **Nf6** and **Be7** are also fine.

deeper.prompt: Time for Black to castle kingside.
deeper.hint: Move the king two squares towards the rook on h8.
deeper.explain: Black's king is safe and the rook is ready. Both sides did the same job.

deeper.prompt: Which is a good reason to stick with one opening?
options: You learn its plans and traps
deeper.explain: Familiar positions mean less guessing and more thinking. That is what really helps you improve.

deeper.title: Famous opening traps
deeper.intro: A king stuck in the middle is in danger. These are the traps that punish it. The second one is a classic.

puzzles.hint: The white king cannot move. Check from a knight cannot be blocked.
puzzles.explain: White's own pieces boxed the king in, and a knight's check cannot be blocked.

puzzles.hint: Black has just taken your queen. Start with a check.
puzzles.explain: This is **Légal's mate**. White gave up the queen so that Black's king would have to step into a net made of minor pieces.
